# Where the stored copy sits: mostly on the line's final token {#sec-storage}

@sec-couplets found that the indirect share that grows with scale sits in the
positions between line 1 and line 2 (the boundary positions), not in the generated
line. Here we locate it token by token, test
whether it is specific to rhymes and to post-training, and compare it with
published accounts.

**Almost all of the copy sits on the line's final token.** In the five runs with a
per-token analysis, the line's final token accounts for 90 to 100% of the boundary
positions' total positive necessity (Qwen3-14B 98%, Qwen3-32B 95% and Gemma 3 27B 93%
with the chat prompt; Gemma 3 12B 90% and 27B 100% with the plain prompt). Necessity is measured one token at a
time over the positions between the rhyme word and line 2. Every boundary token is
reset to its clean state in turn, with the rhyme word edited (@fig-sites A).

- In Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B with the chat prompt, the stored copy sits entirely on
  the comma that ends line 1, with necessity \(+2.09\) [1.50, 2.79] and \(+2.02\)
  [1.46, 2.67]. Every chat-template token (`<|im_end|>`, the role header, the empty
  think block, the newlines) is \(0.00\pm0.03\) by both measures.
- Gemma 3 27B shows the same site: the comma has necessity \(+3.45\) [2.03, 5.05], and
  the other boundary tokens are 0.00 to 0.11, with intervals that include zero.
- With the plain prompt, where line 1 ends in a newline, the copy moves to the
  newline. In Gemma 3 12B the newline has necessity \(+0.68\) [0.41, 0.98] and the
  comma \(+0.07\). In Gemma 3 27B, where the copy is necessary for 74% of persistence,
  it sits entirely on the newline (\(+19.7\) [18.1, 21.4]; the comma \(0.00\)).

The storage site is therefore not a fixed token type. It is the last token of the
line, whatever that token is. This is the position at which @lindsey2025biology
observed Claude's rhyme plan being formed.

**The copy appears from about 12 to 14B parameters, and the base checkpoints we tested have it too.** @tbl-storage gives the copy's
share of persistence by both measures (bottom row of @fig-couplets).

- In Qwen3 the copy is absent up to 8B (necessity at most 0.9% of persistence in
  either format). It appears at 14B: 8% of persistence in the chat format and 16% in
  the plain format, by necessity. It remains at 32B (11% and 13%).
- In Gemma 3 it is absent at 1B and 4B, small at 12B (1 to 3%), and present at 27B:
  11% by necessity in the chat format, and in the plain format 37% by sufficiency and 74% by necessity (\(+19.8\) [18.2, 21.5] of \(+26.9\)). The plain format at 27B is the one configuration in which more of the plan is read from the line's final token than from the rhyme word (19%): a near-complete hand-off to the stored copy, while relay stays at 1%.
- The base checkpoints store it as well. Qwen3-14B-Base stores 16% by sufficiency,
  against 13% for the instruct model in the same format; Gemma 3 12B PT stores 5%
  and 6% against 2% and 3%. Qwen3-8B-Base, like the 8B instruct model, stores
  nothing. In the three base checkpoints tested, the copy is present wherever the
  matching instruct model has it, so it most likely arises in pretraining rather than
  from instruction tuning.
- With same-rhyme donors, the stored copy vanishes (\(-0.02\) to \(+0.01\) at 8B
  to 32B, against \(+0.06\) to \(+1.72\) with different-rhyme donors). It encodes the
  rhyme, not the disruption of the edit.

**Where paths interact, the copy matters more than its sufficiency suggests.** In Gemma 3 27B with the chat
prompt, the stored copy alone moves the rhyme by only \(+0.68\), yet resetting it
removes \(+4.87\) [3.18, 6.73] of a persistence of \(+43.1\). The additivity gap is
29% of persistence (Qwen3 at most 5%). The target combines the rhyme word and the
copy. When only one of them is edited, it reads conflicting evidence and moves less
than the two effects would suggest. This is redundant storage: a second lookup site
that backs up the first. Reporting sufficiency alone would miss most of it. Shapley
values, the average of the two measures, are given in Appendix @sec-app-couplets.

**Reconciling published accounts.** Accounts of rhyme planning disagree on where
the plan lives. The disagreement dissolves once both lookup sites are measured.

- @hanna2026latent find that attention heads near the end of line 2 read the rhyme
  word, and that blocking them breaks rhyming up to 14B. In our terms this is direct
  retrieval together with the late lookup, which dominate at every Qwen3 size.
- @lindsey2025biology find Claude's plan at the newline ending line 1, and @maar2026plan
  steer successfully at the end of the line. This is the stored copy, which appears
  in larger models.
- @ma2026plan patch single layers in plain-text couplets. They report a hand-off from
  the rhyme word to the newline in Gemma 3 27B only, and none in Qwen3-32B. Our
  plain-format measurements agree: Gemma 3 27B reads more of the plan from the stored
  copy (37%) than from the rhyme word (19%). Qwen3-32B keeps a partial copy (10 to
  13%), which a single-layer patch of the naturally computed state can plausibly
  miss.
- @jacopin2026improvisation finds no newline effect at 0.6B to 2.6B. We also find
  no copy below 8B.

Each account is correct for the configuration it studies. The proportions of the two
sites depend on scale, family and prompt format.

**Why the stored copy is not counted as relay.** The stored copy reaches the target
through an intermediate position, as relay does. It differs in three ways. It is
written once, into a fixed structural position of the prompt next to the source. It is
read directly by the target, however much text intervenes. And it does not move with
generation. For a monitor, it is one more place to read, not a path that runs through
the model's output. We therefore count it as a lookup, and keep the name relay for the
path along the generated text.
